Fundamental — what it's worth: A weighted what-if off the published fair value — not a re-run DCF, and it never touches the Monte Carlo section below. The sizes are quick reads off the study’s own sensitivity grids, each of which re-runs the whole backlog-driven build. Note which lever dominates: the terminal cost of capital — because 77.5% of the enterprise value sits in the terminal block, and the study says that plainly rather than hiding it. The second biggest is whether the sales machine keeps running at all: the study computes a run-off that sells NOTHING new after the current backlog and still lands at AED 3.78, above the market price — that gap between the wind-down reading and the tape is the whole thesis.
Technical & price structure: In plain terms: Modon has already sold AED 65.4 billion of property it has not yet built or handed over — the contracted backlog, 95% of it development sales, converting into revenue on a schedule this study models year by year. Capitalise that conversion plus a continuing sales machine and the cash-flow lens says AED 3.54 a share; assume the company never sells another dirham after the current book and the wind-down says AED 2.64. The earnings lenses sit lower still (AED 1.46–2.20). The weighted central is AED 2.50, about 12% BELOW the market price of AED 2.83. That is a reversal, and it is worth saying why. Two earlier editions read this stock as roughly 19% cheap. The difference is not the business — not one revenue line, margin or backlog figure has changed. It is that those editions could not obtain the exchange's official index and measured how much the share moves with the market against a basket built from our own coverage, flagged both times as a stand-in. The official index has since been obtained, and measured properly — including the correction a stock with 84.75% of its shares in one holder requires — Modon is markedly more sensitive to the market than the stand-in implied. The required return rises from 9.1% to 12.6%, and a higher required return makes the same future cash worth less today. The stand-in had been flattering the company. The bet is still conversion: receivables at 440 days of revenue have to actually collect, and the H1-2026 release — AED 26 billion of sales in six months — is the evidence the machine is running.
Monte Carlo — where could the price go?: Our weighted fair value of AED 2.50 sits BELOW the middle of the simulated three-month cone (AED 2.86), between its 5th and 25th percentiles. Read that gap for what it is: the simulation prices where the price can drift on its own volatility over three months, the study prices what the business is worth as the backlog converts. The two are different objects on different clocks and are never blended — and note the cone is unchanged from the previous edition, because the forecast that produced it did not change. Only the fair value moved. A sustained beta reading near the bottom of its range (1.09), or a backlog and collection surprise in the next results release, is where we’d rebuild the study.

One Monte Carlo model, 50,000 paths, driven by the outside forces relevant to an Abu Dhabi master developer: off-plan sales pace and the mortgage-affordability effect of the EIBOR path, the backlog conversion and handover schedule, oil price and the UAE fiscal impulse behind it, population and visa-reform inflows into Abu Dhabi housing, construction-cost inflation on the unrecognised backlog, the pipeline flowing from the IHC ecosystem it sits inside, the Ras El Hekma exposure in Egypt with its own currency risk, hospitality seasonality, and a free float thin enough to move on modest volume. How is the MODON valuation calculated? — The study uses an instrument-appropriate lens — a three-statement FCFF DCF built ground-up from the company's own disclosed AED 65.4bn contracted backlog, rolled off on a conversion schedule, with new sales, development margin, receivable days and payables-and-advances cover each projected as its own driver — cross-checked against relative multiples on an attributable-earnings basis, normalised earnings power and a justified price-to-book. A run-off case that sells nothing new after the current backlog is computed alongside the base case and published side by side, never averaged. Combined with a 50,000-path Monte Carlo simulation that expresses the near-term as a probability distribution. Every assumption is visible and editable in the free Excel model.

Does testahil recommend buying or selling MODON? — No. testahil never issues buy, sell, or hold recommendations. It publishes fair-value ranges and probability distributions as educational material, and grades its own forecasts publicly when they resolve.
